steps.title: Pass, distinction, or try again?
steps.body:
Every results portal makes decisions: *if* marks are 90 or more, show a distinction; *otherwise if* 60 or more, a pass. Java decides with `if` / `else if` / `else`, and one rule about the order catches out a lot of students.

In five minutes you’ll trace a decision, spot that trap, and write a condition yourself.

options.why: An if / else-if / else chain runs exactly ONE branch, never all of them.
72 >= 60 is true, so the B branch runs.
else only runs when nothing above it was true, and marks >= 60 was true.
Right. The first true condition wins, only its block runs, then the program continues.

steps.title: How if / else works
points: A condition is a **boolean**: true or false. Compare with `==  !=  <  <=  >  >=`.
In an `if / else if / else` chain the **first true branch wins** and the rest are skipped.
`=` stores a value and `==` compares. Mixing them up is the most common beginner bug.

steps.prompt: A classic trap. What does this print?

options.why: It compiles fine; the order of the conditions is the bug, and the compiler cannot spot it.
Yes. The first true branch wins. Because the >= 60 test comes first, a 95 never gets to the distinction check.
Only one branch of the chain runs.
95 >= 60 is checked FIRST, and it is true, so Distinction can never be reached. Put the strictest test first.

steps.prompt: Your turn. Write the condition that is true exactly when n is even. We'll also try it with other values of n.
steps.hint: An even number leaves no remainder when divided by 2.
steps.explain: `n % 2 == 0` is true exactly when dividing by 2 leaves nothing over, which is what "even" means.
